target_audience: University students in Computer Science or Cybersecurity

sections.title: The Privacy Paradox
sections.content: Introduction to the challenge of contact tracing: How can we track exposure to a virus without creating a 'Big Brother' surveillance state? Contrast the Centralized model (where a server knows everyone's location) with the Decentralized (DP-3T) model.
sections.example: Imagine two animals, Pip the Penguin and Leo the Lion, passing each other in a forest. They want to be able to warn each other if they get sick later, but they don't want a 'Forest King' server to know exactly when or where they met.

sections.title: Prerequisite: One-Way Hash Functions
sections.content: Explanation of cryptographic hashing and seeds. Visualizing a 'Secret Shaker': you put a secret key in, and it generates a unique, unpredictable string of numbers. Crucially, you can't go backwards from the numbers to the key.
sections.example: A mathematical 'blender' icon: Inputting a 'Seed of the Day' produces a sequence of 'Rolling Codes' that look like random noise to anyone watching.

sections.title: The Daily Secret & Rolling IDs
sections.content: Every day, Pip’s phone generates a 'Secret Day Key' (SKt). From this key, the phone derives 'Rolling Proximity Identifiers' (RPIs) that change every 15 minutes. This prevents someone from tracking Pip throughout the day using a static ID.
sections.example: Pip’s phone broadcasts 'A12B' at 10:00 AM and 'C99X' at 10:15 AM. To Leo, these look like two completely different strangers.

sections.title: The Digital Handshake (Log Storage)
sections.content: When Pip and Leo are close, their phones exchange these RPIs via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). Each phone stores the IDs it *hears* in a local, encrypted 'Diary' folder. No location data (GPS) is ever recorded.
sections.example: Leo’s phone 'hears' Pip's RPI and whispers to its internal storage: 'I saw code A12B today at a signal strength of -70dB.' Leo’s phone doesn't know this code belongs to Pip.

sections.title: Sounding the Alarm: The Diagnosis Upload
sections.content: If Pip tests positive, he uploads his 'Secret Day Keys' for the last 14 days to a central server. Note: He does NOT upload his contacts. The server only hosts a list of 'Sick Keys'—not identities.
sections.example: Pip sends his 'Secret Day Key' (the seed) to a public bulletin board. The board shows: 'The owner of the seed that produced these codes is sick,' but the board doesn't know who Pip met.

sections.title: Local Matching: The Private Detective
sections.content: Every phone periodically downloads the new 'Sick Keys' from the server. Leo's phone uses these keys to recreate all possible RPIs that the sick person *would* have broadcasted. It then compares these to the codes in its local 'Diary'.
sections.example: Leo's phone runs the 'Secret Shaker' math on Pip's uploaded key. It generates 'A12B'. It checks the Diary, finds 'A12B', and alerts Leo: 'You were near someone who is now sick!'

sections.title: Summary: Privacy by Design
sections.content: Recap of why DP-3T is secure: 1. Identities stay on devices. 2. The server never sees the 'Handshake'. 3. All matching happens locally. The math ensures that even the government can't reconstruct the social graph.
sections.example: A split-screen visual: On the left, a Centralized 'Web' connecting everyone. On the right, DP-3T shows isolated dots that only connect momentarily on their own terms.
